content: 1. Ensure that all healthcare staff receive comprehensive training on the correct use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including donning, doffing, and disposal procedures, to minimize the risk of contamination and infection. 2. Maintain an adequate supply of appropriate PPE, such as disinfectable cotton gowns, and ensure that reusable items are properly disinfected after each use to prevent cross-contamination. 3. Avoid reusing disposable PPE items, as the safety and efficacy of reusing such items are not well-established and may increase the risk of infection for healthcare workers. 4. Provide training to users on the proper use of particulate respirators, including how to perform a seal check every time the respirator is worn, to prevent contamination during use. Ensure proper removal and disposal of respirators after use. 5. When caring for multiple patients with similar respiratory infections (e.g., pulmonary tuberculosis) in a cohort setting, healthcare workers may wear a single particulate respirator for the duration of the activity, provided it is not removed or touched during use. If the respirator becomes wet or soiled, it must be replaced immediately. 6. If particulate respirators are unavailable, avoid performing aerosol-generating procedures that carry a high risk of pathogen transmission in patients with acute respiratory infections (ARIs) of concern. 7. Medical masks should be worn tightly fitted to the face and discarded immediately after use. If a mask becomes wet or soiled, it must be replaced promptly. 8. In cases of novel ARIs with unknown transmission modes, implement the highest level of infection prevention and control (IPC) precautions, including the use of particulate respirators, until the mode of transmission is clarified. 9. Gloves should be reserved for situations where contact with blood, respiratory secretions, or body fluids is likely, particularly during aerosol-generating procedures. Gloves must be changed between patients, and hand hygiene should still be performed, as glove use does not eliminate the need for proper hand hygiene. 10. Gowns may be worn when caring for multiple patients in a single cohort area, provided the gown does not come into direct contact with any patient. Reusable eye protection, such as goggles or face shields, must be cleaned and decontaminated according to the manufacturer’s instructions after each use. 11. Conventional eyeglasses should not be used as eye protection, as they do not provide adequate protection against splashes to the eye mucosa. 12. PPE should provide additional protection for the user without increasing risks to others or the environment. If PPE reuse is unavoidable, it must be done under safe conditions. Unnecessary use of PPE should be avoided. 13. When removing a deceased body from an isolation room, ensure proper use of PPE to avoid direct contact with body fluids. If the family wishes to view the body, they may do so under standard precautions, including the use of appropriate PPE. 14. During postmortem examinations, ensure safety measures are in place, such as performing the procedure in a well-ventilated room and using appropriate PPE. Minimize the number of staff involved and ensure they are adequately trained in IPC measures. 15. Autopsies should be conducted in rooms with effective ventilation systems to reduce aerosol generation. Surfaces should be disinfected with appropriate solutions, allowing sufficient contact time, and rinsed thoroughly. 16. Healthcare facilities should establish permanent IPC activities, surveillance, and training programs for staff. A multidisciplinary team should develop and regularly update a preparedness plan for communicable disease emergencies. 17. Early detection systems and safe care practices should be continuously strengthened to prepare for ARI epidemics or pandemics. Routine promotion of standard precautions in healthcare is essential to reduce pathogen transmission. 18. Surveillance systems within healthcare facilities should prioritize early recognition and investigation of potential pandemic ARI cases. Hospitals should be connected to public health surveillance systems to report cases promptly. 19. Define IPC measures for triage, patient flow, and placement to prevent ARI transmission. Promptly initiate IPC precautions when an epidemic or pandemic ARI is suspected. 20. Plan for surge capacity by estimating the impact of a potential pandemic on healthcare resources, including supplies, infrastructure, and staffing. Develop strategies for alternative care sites and supplemental staffing. 21. Establish environmental and engineering controls, such as effective ventilation and cleaning protocols, to reduce the risk of ARI transmission in healthcare settings. 22. Consider vaccination against new ARI agents of concern if a vaccine is available. Emphasize surveillance among healthcare workers to detect early signs of human-to-human transmission. 23. Provide psychosocial support to healthcare workers and plan staff reassignment based on risk assessments. Ensure infected healthcare workers receive appropriate treatment and follow-up. 24. Develop strategies to manage patient flow and discharge planning during outbreaks to prevent ARI transmission. Separate high-risk patients, such as the immunocompromised and elderly, from those with known or suspected ARIs. 25. Plan for mass fatalities, including culturally and religiously sensitive burial practices, and ensure adequate mortuary capacity during pandemics. 26. Limit unnecessary office visits by ill patients by diverting them to designated triage and evaluation sites. Use pre-arrival triage to determine which patients require on-site medical evaluation. 27. Address research gaps in ARI transmission and IPC practices, including the effectiveness of interventions, cost implications, and social factors affecting compliance. Conduct high-quality studies to inform future IPC strategies.
